Package net.sourceforge.plantuml.regex

Class FirstTokens

java.lang.Object
net.sourceforge.plantuml.regex.FirstTokens
public final class FirstTokens extends Object
Reads, from a command pattern alone, the first tokens a line must start with for that pattern to have any chance of matching it -- so that the regex stays the only place a command says what it accepts, instead of repeating it in a hand-written declaration that nothing keeps in sync. The token is the one StringLocated#getFirstToken computes, once the blanks the line may open with are skipped:
  • the leading run of ASCII letters, lower-cased, for a line starting with a letter;
  • the first character alone, for a line starting with anything else -- ""}, "-", "#", each digit on its own...;
  • "" for a blank line.
Case is not an issue: the patterns are compiled with CASE_INSENSITIVE and without UNICODE_CASE, which folds exactly the ASCII letters the token itself folds, and nothing else.

Everything here leans the same way on purpose. Returning a token too many only costs the regex attempt it could have saved, while returning one too few makes a command unreachable for the lines it left out, so every step that cannot be followed exactly is either widened or given up on: from(String) answers null -- "I cannot tell" -- and the command then declares nothing and stays in the list tried for every line.

Two things a reader will want to have in mind, because they are what most of the care below is about:

  • a token is not over until a non-letter arrives, so ^end[%s]*split$ does not describe a line starting with end: [%s]* matches nothing at all, and endsplit is a line this pattern accepts. An element that may be empty therefore leaves the token open for whatever follows to extend;
  • a blank the line opens with is skipped by the token reader -- the blanks being those of StringUtils#isTrimmable, U+00A0 included, which is exactly what %s stands for. A blank therefore contributes nothing while the line may still be in its leading blanks, and only closes the token once one has started. A character class that may be a blank or something else, like [%s,], is read both ways;
  • any other character, met where the line may still be in its leading blanks, is a token of its own. That is why a character class, \d included, must be read as the exact set of characters it holds: each of them is a token the command may start with. The ASCII letters of a class, as in [hx]-axis, are read one by one like any other letter. A class that cannot be enumerated -- negated, %pLN, \w... -- makes the whole pattern unknown;
  • a lookahead or a lookbehind only rules lines out, so it is read past as if it were not there: the worst it can cost is a token too many.

      Whether two declarations of first tokens say the same thing: both null -- "any line" -- or the same tokens, whatever their order and whatever kind of collection holds them. A Set and a List of the same tokens are not equals(), yet they declare exactly the same: this is what a hand-written list is to be compared with.
